persons.name: J. Garland
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'J. GARLAND' and the corpus reads his trade as cooper. Cited at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a cooper and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - fourth of 4 cooper households in this layer, in the north division. A TOWN PACKING THOUSANDS OF HOGS A SEASON NEEDS COOPERS, AND THIS DATASET HELD NONE. Andreas records that Clybourne packed some 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs in the season of 1833, that George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place, and that the Newberry & Dole house on the South Branch packed 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in 1834 (scan p. 1151). Packed provisions travel in barrels and barrels are made by coopers. The documented layer holds a packer, two slaughter-houses and not one cooper. Four cooper households are inferred against the schedule's six W3 cooper, wagon or wheelwright shops. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Garland, a documented cooper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.

persons.name: G. W. Keeney
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'G. W. KEENEY' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 7 May 1834, column 3. The corpus associates the name with Chicago; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `founder` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name G. W. Keeney as a founder at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

The 1840 Chicago schedule counts children under ten at 27% of the town and women of twenty to twenty-nine as its second-largest band; the 1835 layer the sources can name holds 15 women, because the rolls that name this town — a letter list, a voters' roll, a subscription — print men. That gap is the shape of the evidence and not a reading of the town, so the order book counts it bucket by bucket and this household is drawn against those counts. Every value on it carries the model row and the seed that redraws it, and a source naming a woman who kept her own house in this division retires the whole record. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1).

citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED / GENERATED, NOT AN ATTESTED NAMED BUILDING. Family and aggregate district role follow the owner-supplied 2026 specification; exact presence, location, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive.

fabric_basis.words: silvered clapboard on a balloon frame, 9-over-6 sash of 6 × 8 in glass and plain corner boards, under a weathered roof — a one-and-a-half-story cottage, a year old (rule F-T: a tradesman's by its type)
